title: Why McLaren have named their rotating wing the 'H-Wing'
excerpt:
McLaren will be looking to continue their run of good form at the upcoming Italian Grand Prix, a weekend in which the team have announced some new parts for the car – including the ‘H-Wing’.

After Ferrari debuted their so-called ‘flip-flop’ rotating rear wing during pre-season testing, Red Bull revealed a version of their own at Round 4 in Miami while McLaren later went on to trial a rotating design during Free Practice 1 in Hungary.

Now the Woking-based outfit are planning to run the wing during the Monza weekend and, in their preview of the event, also explained why it has been called the ‘H-Wing’.

“The H-Wing’s naming convention pays homage to McLaren’s innovative F-duct, which debuted in 2010 and took its name from the ‘F’ in the branding positioned alongside the system’s inlet on the car,” the preview reads.

“In the same spirit, the H-Wing is named after the ‘H’ in Etihad Airways branding displayed on the rear wing as part of the team’s partnership with the airline.”

McLaren stated that they will also introduce some “minor aerodynamic updates” at the Italian Grand Prix, as well as using “previously declared parts that are specific for such a unique track layout”.

Neil Houldey, Technical Director of Applied Engineering at the team, said ahead of the weekend: “Monza presents a unique challenge, with its long straights placing a premium on drag reduction, while the heavy braking zones demand stability and the chicanes require good ride performance.

“Energy will also be limited around the lap, so understanding the best way to recharge and deploy it will be an important focus during practice. Managing overtakes will therefore be particularly important, as different approaches to harvesting and deploying energy could create a yo-yo effect, with cars trading an advantage at different points around the lap.

“That said, the margins at the front remain extremely tight, so the accuracy of our pre-event simulation and simulator work will be critical in giving us a strong baseline. From there, we need clean practice sessions to refine the car and maximise the car-and-driver combination.

“This weekend, we have brought what we believe is needed to be competitive, including a new low-drag rear wing specification, including the first use of our H-Wing, alongside some small aerodynamic and low-drag options that we will evaluate before deciding the final specification for Qualifying.

“Overall, we know there is still more performance to unlock from the MCL40, both through maximising the package we already have and through further upgrades planned for the races ahead.”

title: Red Bull sign long-serving Aston Martin engineer
excerpt:
Long-time Aston Martin figure Tom McCullough is set to join Red Bull Racing in 2027 as their Head of Racing, it has been announced.

McCullough will make the move after a lengthy stint with Aston Martin and their previous guises, Racing Point and Force India, where he worked in various engineering roles.

At the start of 2025, as part of a senior leadership restructure, he was moved away from the Aston Martin F1 project and into another area of the business that focused on “the expansion of the team’s broader range of racing categories”.

Last month, it emerged that McCullough would be leaving Aston Martin at the end of the 2026 season, with his future plans unclear.

However, ahead of this weekend’s Italian Grand Prix, Red Bull communicated McCullough’s impending arrival as the Milton Keynes-based squad look to rebuild their own senior leadership structure following several high-profile exits.

Max Verstappen’s Race Engineer, Gianpiero Lambiase, is one of the most recent examples, with the Briton due to leave Red Bull when his current contract expires in 2028 and join McLaren as their Chief Racing Officer.

“We’re delighted to welcome Tom to the team at the beginning of 2027 and look forward to the wealth of experience and expertise he will bring to the role,” read a brief statement from Red Bull.

McCullough started his F1 career at Williams back in the early 2000s, spending around a decade with the outfit and then following up a brief spell at Sauber with a move to Force India.

title: What's still to play for in the F1 driver market?
excerpt:
We've seen more driver market dominos fall in the last couple of weeks, with Max Verstappen confirming he's staying put at Red Bull not just for next season but until the end of 2030, while Alpine announced last week they've re-signed Franco Colapinto alongside Pierre Gasly. So what's still to play for and who holds the key?

Most teams are choosing stability rather than trying something new and thus we've seen a host of renewals rather than unveilings of new faces of late.

McLaren are sorted for next year with Lando Norris – who recently extended his deal by a few years to keep him at the team until at least the end of 2030 – alongside Oscar Piastri, while Ferrari are sticking with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

title: Aron set for next FP1 run with Alpine at Monza
excerpt:
Alpine have confirmed that reserve driver Paul Aron will participate in another Free Practice 1 outing for the squad at this weekend’s Italian Grand Prix.

Aron has previously been in action during three practice sessions so far in 2026, with the first in Barcelona and Austria being with Audi as part of an agreement between the two teams.

The Estonian went on to drive for Alpine in Hungary and will again get behind the wheel of the A526 when Friday’s track running kicks off in Monza, sitting in for Pierre Gasly.

From there Aron will embark on a busy weekend, as he will head back to the team’s Enstone base for simulator work in the evening after his FP1 run in order to help with fine-tuning the car’s set-up.

“I am looking forward to driving again in Free Practice 1 with the team this weekend,” said Aron. “I am grateful to the team for giving me the opportunity to get back behind the wheel so soon.

“I was very pleased with my session in Budapest, and I hope to build on it this time around, particularly helping the team compare our latest upgrade package which I have driven in the simulator.

“It's going to be a busy weekend for me as I'll be on the simulator at Enstone on Friday night to further help the team fine tune the set-up before returning to the track on Saturday. I'll give it my all to hopefully assist the team in having a successful weekend.”

The weekend at Monza will also see both Gasly and Franco Colapinto run the upgrade package that was first introduced on Gasly’s car last time out in Zandvoort.

title: What do McLaren’s newest upgrades tell us ahead of Monza?
excerpt:
On top of Hungary’s all-new floor, wakeboards and floor slots, McLaren brought to Zandvoort a new rear wing, engine cover, diffuser tweaks and new front wheel rims as further discrete performance items.

“The items aren’t linked as a package,” explained McLaren’s technical director Neil Houldey of the Zandvoort parts. “They all provide aero performance as individual components and don’t need each other to perform.”

This double hit of upgrades in consecutive races proved very powerful and helped Lando Norris to back-to-back Grand Prix victories, both of them from pole position.

title: Ferrari reveal special Schumacher-inspired livery for Monza
excerpt:
Ferrari have presented a special one-off livery for their home race at Monza, paying tribute to seven-time World Champion Michael Schumacher.

It is now 30 years since the German joined the Scuderia, and 20 years since his final victory with the team – scored at the 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

As well as claiming five of his world titles with the Maranello-based squad, Schumacher bagged five Monza wins in red (in 1996, 1998, 2000, 2003 and 2006).

Heading into the weekend, Ferrari revealed bespoke race suits that will be worn by current drivers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, featuring Schumacher’s logo and the seven stars he used to carry on his helmet to signify his seven titles.

On Tuesday morning, the outfit followed up on those comments by showcasing a Schumacher-inspired car livery, again noting the details above around their usual 2026 design.

Ferrari explained that this week’s wide-ranging tributes are inspired by Schumacher’s “impact on the racing world” and “his enduring mindset”.

title: 7 memorable Italian Grand Prix moments from Monza
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix is only a few days away, and Monza is ready to welcome the teams, drivers and fans in typical Italian fashion. From teary moments to the Tifosi showing up in style, the fastest circuit in Formula 1 has never lacked entertainment on or off the track.

Monza was on the F1 calendar from the very beginning and has hosted all Italian Grands Prix but one since 1950. Here are some of the most unforgettable moments from the Temple of Speed in recent racing history...

Leclerc delights the Tifosi

There's arguably nothing more special for an F1 driver than winning for Ferrari on home soil at Monza – something Charles Leclerc acheived in 2019 when he topped the podium in Italy, taking his second career win in Formula 1 and his first at Monza.

“There were people as far as I could see,” he said afterwards. “It was packed. I was trying to find my mum. She was in a grandstand... I was trying to find her but there were way too many people.”

Schumacher equals Senna's tally

No driver has won more races for Ferrari than the great Michael Schumacher, but perhaps one of his most emotional victories was in the 2000 Italian Grand Prix?

After missing the previous year’s Grand Prix, the German driver returned to Monza in top shape, winning the race in front of the Tifosi. It was his 41st career victory, meaning he equalled the tally Ayrton Senna – something a very emotional Schumacher was reminded about in the post-race press conference.

Ferrari turns 90

Ferrari chose the weekend of the Italian Grand Prix to celebrate their 90th anniversary in 2019, when they took over Piazza Duomo in Milan to hold a special “90 years of emotions” event which saw Charles Leclerc and Sebastian Vettel alongside drivers and management from the past, marking the storied history of the Maranello team in front of a sea of red jerseys and caps with the iconic Duomo di Milano as a backdrop.

The Tifosi gather at the Piazza Duomo during the “90 Years of Emotion” event in 2019

A host of former Ferrari drivers were in attendance

Piazza Duomo was the setting for Ferrari's 90th year celebration

A maiden victory for Gasly

Monza without grandstands packed with passionate supporters is almost impossible to imagine. But in 2020 – due to the Covid pandemic – the Italian Grand Prix was held behind closed doors, and in an empty venue, Pierre Gasly found his way to success.

The French driver, wearing the colours of the other Italian team – then known as AlphaTauri – raced to his first ever Formula 1 victory.

Vettel's first triumph

But Gasly's win in 2020 wasn't the first time a driver from 'Italy's other team' had raced to a maiden victory at Monza.

Sebastian Vettel was in just his first full season as an F1 driver when he claimed a shock pole position for Toro Rosso at the Italian Grand Prix – and then followed that up with his first ever win.

The shoey returns

The Italian Grand Prix holds a special place in Daniel Ricciardo’s heart. The Australian won at Monza for McLaren in 2021, three years after his last victory. But it wasn’t a lucky win – Ricciardo led the race from start to finish and after a 1,204-day wait, he was back on the top of the podium ahead of his team mate Lando Norris, and Valtteri Bottas.

And what a better way to celebrate the long-awaited win with the iconic shoey celebration including Norris and McLaren boss Zak Brown?

Hamilton arriving in Monza in style

More recently, Sir Lewis Hamilton wanted to show up in style for his first Italian Grand Prix as a Ferrari driver – and he did not disappoint.

The seven-time world champion arrived at the circuit for last year's event riding a motorbike in the colours of the Italian flag.

He went on to finish sixth in that race, but will be hoping he can challenge for victory this weekend, after he took his first Grand Prix win in red earlier this year in Barcelona.

title: Mercedes urged to consider George Russell Italian GP grid penalty
excerpt:
Former Formula 1 driver David Coulthard has urged Mercedes to consider changing George Russell's power unit at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has already confirmed that championship leader Kimi Antonelli will take a grid penalty at Monza, with a full engine change to take place.

This will see engine components outside of the Italian's legal pool fitted to his W17, while Russell is also on the cusp of needing to take a grid penalty.

The British driver is on his last legal exhaust, internal combustion engine, turbocharger, energy store and power control electronics unit, meaning a grid drop is effectively inevitable unless he can get through the rest of the season without needing a new component.

Monza is a venue where teams often choose to serve a grid penalty and fit new engine parts, due to the opportunities it offers to overtake and recover positions.

With its strong power unit, Antonelli is expected to make up good ground even from the back of the grid, although Mercedes' customer teams, particularly McLaren, are catching up.

With the upcoming races in Madrid and Baku both being street venues, taking a grid penalty would be challenging, making Coulthard wonder if the Silver Arrows should also fit new parts to Russell's car this weekend.

Discussing Russell also likely needing to take a grid penalty soon, Coulthard told the Up to Speed podcast: "Yeah, I think you've just got to cut a stick when you see it.

"I don't know where that expression comes from, but you have to take a penalty. Monza, as we've said, let's say, offers more potential.

"They have a good power unit deployment understanding. That was what gave them such an advantage over the other Mercedes teams like McLaren and Williams and Alpine at the beginning of the year.

"I think that is where McLaren have made some of the biggest strides, understanding how to use the power unit, and we will find out very soon who comes out victorious from that particular race."

title: Italian GP trophies revealed as 'ancient tradition' incorporated
excerpt:
The podium finishers at this year's Italian Grand Prix will lift something rather different from the usual silverware.

FRAGILE, a trophy conceived by Italian artistic duo vedovamazzei, is the centrepiece of the 2026 edition of a multi-year project that sees a new Italian artist commissioned to design the Monza race trophy each year.

The project, now in its sixth edition, was initiated by Pirelli, the race's title sponsor, in partnership with the Pirelli HangarBicocca Museum of Contemporary Art. It represents an ongoing effort to intertwine the world of Formula 1 with contemporary Italian art.

This year's commission fell to vedovamazzei, the duo formed by Stella Scala and Simeone Crispino. Their practice is characterised by the use of irony and an ability to expose the contradictions and complexities of everyday reality, frequently through the reinterpretation of ordinary objects.

FRAGILE takes its form from a vertical stack of household objects, cups and small bowls piled upon one another in a composition that appears deliberately unsteady. The visual tension between grandeur and instability is entirely intentional.

The production process combined traditional craftsmanship with modern technology. Initial drawings and sketches were transferred onto paper before a 3D printing process using nylon powder was employed to produce the physical form. The material was subsequently painted, galvanised, and polished to a reflective finish.

The 2026 commission continues a lineage of artistic collaborations that includes Alice Ronchi (2021), Patrick Tuttofuoco (2022), Ruth Beraha (2023), Andrea Sala (2024), and Nico Vascellari (2025).

"The idea for the trophy stems from the ancient tradition of passing a celebratory cup from hand to hand. It served as a large drinking vessel, creating a sense of shared celebration and festivity," vedovamazzei explained.

"We wanted the trophy to be the symbol of a victory that an individual holds in their hands, yet it reflects the spirit of a community. In the case of Formula 1, this community includes the team, the fans, and the entire world revolving around the drivers.

"The composition also evokes an everyday dimension with its repeated gestures, suggesting a victory earned lap after lap that never corresponds to an eternal, unchanging status. It is unstable, short-lived, and must be reclaimed. In fact, it is fragile."

title: Tropical Italian Grand Prix temperatures to trigger F1 engines test
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix weekend at Monza is shaping up to be a genuinely sweltering affair, with dry and sunny conditions expected throughout, and temperatures climbing to as high as 33 degrees Celsius across the three days.

Friday's opening free practice session gets underway at 12:30 PM under full sunshine, with the thermometer already sitting at around 30 degrees.

By the time FP2 rolls around at 4:00 PM, conditions will have intensified to approximately 32 degrees, with only a light to moderate westerly wind offering any meaningful relief for those out on the circuit and in the paddock.

Saturday brings more of the same. FP3 will be run in around 32 degrees of heat before qualifying at 4:00 PM, where temperatures could peak at 33 degrees. That is exceptionally warm for this time of year, even by the standards of the traditional late-summer Italian Grand Prix slot on the calendar.

One factor that will demand close attention from every team on the grid is track temperature. Intense sunshine heats the asphalt considerably beyond the ambient air temperature, and the resulting high track temps will have a direct bearing on tyre behaviour, degradation rates, and the ability of the power units to keep themselves adequately cooled. It is a variable that could well influence strategic thinking across the weekend.

Sunday's race begins at 3:00 PM, and the forecast remains consistent: sunny, dry, and approximately 32 degrees at the start, with a light easterly to south-easterly breeze. Rain is not anticipated at any point, meaning the teams can plan around a fully dry weekend without concern for a sudden shift in conditions.

title: Charles Leclerc points to unleashed Ferrari 'aggression' in rapidly-changing F1 war
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc believes Ferrari's "aggressive" upgrade approach in 2026 is "very impressive" as the team looks to mount a charge for the F1 titles.

The SF-26 machine of Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton finds itself 87 points behind Mercedes in the constructors' standings heading into the Scuderia's home Italian GP, with Hamilton in a tie for second place in the drivers' standings, 59 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli and behind George Russell only on countback by dint of Russell holding two wins to Hamilton's one.

Unlike Mercedes, Ferrari has been delivering constant upgrades to the car, including packages in Miami, Barcelona, Austria, Britain, Hungary, and last time out in the Netherlands, with a further engine upgrade, making the most from its ADUO tokens, expected for its home race in Monza.

In contrast, Mercedes has been slow in bringing upgrades, not doing so since May's Canadian GP, with McLaren also reeling in Mercedes.

However, Leclerc feels the "aggressive" attack from the production office in Maranello and innovative ideas from the design office, such as the Macarena rear-wing and small exhaust tailpipe winglet, mean the team is on a sound footing.

"There is a very clear development programme, and there are still many things that we want to improve," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365.

"It is very clear what the main limitations from the first part of the season are. The engine and power that we have at the moment compared to Mercedes and Red Bull is where we are lacking the most, and that is where our focus is.

"There's an engine, and a chassis and aero teams, but the programme is set, and we know where we want to go, and that is a good thing. I don't think we've had particularly bad surprises in the first half of the season, which with the previous generation of car, with it touching the ground, was difficult.

"Sometimes, you wouldn't get what you had in a wind-tunnel, and we don't really have that this year, and that is very positive for the development of future things we want to bring to the car.

"It's very impressive. We've had a very aggressive approach this year compared to others. I believe first in terms of innovation, and I think this is a very positive sign to see that shows that we are innovating and getting out of our way to try and find solutions around the regulations.

"And second, the aggressive, the very aggressive plan of bringing upgrades. I think production has done an incredible job for that first half of the season to work flat out in order for us to receive the parts as early as possible.

"It's making a lot of difference in a year like this where we are so early in the development, and every upgrade you bring makes such a big difference, so we'll continue pushing like that for that second part of the season."

title: Helmut Marko highlights 'crucial factor' behind Max Verstappen contract extension
excerpt:
Max Verstappen's new deal with Red Bull until 2030 has brought months of speculation over the four-time F1 drivers' champion's future to a definitive end, and Helmut Marko believes the timing could not have been better.

The extension, announced on Thursday ahead of Verstappen's home Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort, commits the 28-year-old to the Milton Keynes-based outfit for what will be a remarkable 15th season with the six-time constructors' champions.

Former Red Bull adviser and head of its young driver programme, Marko, was responsible for bringing Verstappen to Red Bull in the first place, and was quick to point out what the 71-time grand prix winner's re-signing will mean for the team.

"It's the right signal at exactly the right time," said Marko to Krone Zeitung.

"This will bring calm and stability to the team, but it's about performance, and emotions run high. The result is what matters most... he will have outlined his conditions."

Verstappen's future had been the subject of intense paddock discussion throughout much of 2025 and into 2026, with performance-related exit clauses in his previous contract, which ran until the end of 2028, opening the door to a potential departure.

McLaren and Mercedes were the two most frequently cited destinations, with informal talks between Verstappen's management and McLaren acknowledged by both sides, and Mercedes boss Toto Wolff admitting to conversations behind closed doors.

Verstappen himself, however, indicated that retirement was a more realistic alternative than switching teams upon his renewal, with the Dutchman openly contemplating life away from Formula 1 after expressing frustrations about elements of the sport.

In the end, he ultimately chose to stay. And for Marko, the implications of that decision stretch far beyond the driver himself.

"Max is the face of the whole team, a leading figure," Marko said before adding that the contract extension is a "crucial factor" as "every ambitious engineer wants to work with the best driver."

The length of the deal is notable. By committing through 2030, Verstappen's contract aligns with the end of the current V6 turbo-hybrid power unit cycle and takes him to the brink of what is widely expected to be Formula 1's next major regulatory shift.

The FIA is targeting a switch to 2.4-litre V8 engines running on fully sustainable fuels, with 2031 the most likely introduction date, although an earlier 2030 start remains a possibility if manufacturers agree.

"Whether a new engine will be introduced in 2030 or 2031 remains to be seen," Marko added. "That certainly played a role."

title: McLaren offers 'in reality' evidence to explain puzzling F1 car trait
excerpt:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella has offered evidence as to why the team's slow-speed corner weakness did not show itself during victories in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Although Lando Norris was able to take pole at both the Hungaroring and in Zandvoort, converting both into dominant victories, he believes the MCL40 machine is struggling in low-speed corners compared to the championship-leading Mercedes W17 of Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

Whilst Norris believes that his car is stronger in the high- and medium-speed corners, it is lacking in the slow-speed ones.

It is a trait which has carried over in the DNA of the McLaren from previous generations of cars, with Norris reporting in the past that slow-speed rotation was an issue for the car whilst high- and medium-speed corners produced better results.

Both the Hungaroring and Zandvoort are regarded as 'slow-speed' circuits, but when questioned why the weakness had not shown itself as Norris enjoyed his back-to-back pole and wins, Stella explained that the "reality" of the Hungaroring, in particular, was different from what is widely believed.

"I think I have clear ideas about part of it; part of it I'm not sure about, so let's start with the part where I have some clear ideas," Stella began to tell media, including RacingNews365, when asked why the slow-speed weakness had not shown itself in Hungary.

"I think when Lando refers to the fact that in the race he can't push the high speed, that's true, but to some extent. I think the main problem in the race is that you can push in the high speed and gain a bit of time, but you won't gain as much as you lose in all the low-speed corners.

"There are many more low-speed corners than high-speed corners at [Zandvoort]. Also, when you are in a race stint compared to qualifying, the duration of a corner at low speed is much longer. You brake much earlier. You go even lower speed, and traction is much longer, so the grip-limited sections, especially at low speed, become much bigger.

"So if you have a deficit in this condition, you can kind of compensate in qualifying because, with low fuel and new rubber, the low-speed corner is still pretty short, but in the race it becomes much, much longer. So I think when you have a deficit in low speed, it's always going to be a bit of a problem on tracks like this, in which there's a dominance of low-speed sections.

"In relation to why this was less important in Hungary, I'm not as clear in my head as to why I think Hungary, which is often classified as a low-speed track, in reality is very much a medium-speed track.

"Like, even corner two is above 120kph, just to give you an idea; corner one and the chicane and probably the penultimate corner are around 100kph, but all the rest is well above 100.

"So I think the speed range is slightly different, and then there are some other things, setup-wise, that you can do in Hungary that you cannot do as much of [at Zandvoort], which I think were a good benefit for our car.

"Now I don't want to disclose too much, but I think there's a speed range difference, and there are some technical differences in how you exploit your car that you can do in Hungary, but you cannot do here."

title: George Russell wary of Mercedes stumble after 'out of sync' upgrade push
excerpt:
George Russell believes Mercedes must "hope" its upgrades to its F1 car "work" when they are finally delivered after falling "out of sync" in the development war.

The W17 has not been given a big upgrade package since May's Canadian Grand Prix, but Mercedes still leads the constructors' by 87 points from Ferrari heading into the Italian GP, whilst Russell is 59 points behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli in second place in the drivers' standings, equal with Lewis Hamilton of Ferrari on 183 points.

Russell is ahead by dint of holding two grands prix wins to Hamilton's one, but a resurgent Lando Norris of McLaren is now 24 points behind Russell, with Antonelli claiming that the McLaren is "now the car to beat" following Norris's dominant Dutch GP win.

Team boss Toto Wolff has claimed that due to the "financial realities" of the cost cap, Mercedes does not have the money to bring upgrades as fast as Ferrari or McLaren are, meaning the team is holding onto its developments before unleashing a big package later in the year.

With the swing in momentum away from the Brackley squad, Russell feels the team must be wary of the upgrades not working "as you expect" when delivered and thus missing out on "big points."

"Given the fact that we’re nowhere near as dominant as we once were, I think this was a very solid weekend all in all," Russell explained about his performance in the Dutch GP last time out to media, including RacingNews365.

"I was not on the podium at times when we had the best car, and Kimi was performing right at the very front. Now, you know, the pace between the two of us looks very similar, and that’s a good step forward for me.

"I’m not dealing with as many issues as I’ve faced at the end of that first half of the season, and it’s just allowing me to focus on the job. But I think these coming two or three race weekends will be a challenge for us both, purely because we’re out of sync with the upgrades.

"There is a long way to go. I think the Ferrari is looking great. Lando’s been on pole for the last two races as well, so you can’t count anybody out.

"We’ve got these upgrades coming. We’ve got to hope that they work. It only takes one issue with an upgrade, and it doesn’t work as you expect, and before you know it, you’re not fighting week in, week out, and there can be big points missed."

title: Lando Norris responds to salary speculation after McLaren F1 extension
excerpt:
Lando Norris has played down how much he is earning as part of his new contract with McLaren.

The reigning champion recently penned a new deal with the Woking-based squad, ensuring he will stay with the team until at least the end of the 2030 season.

Shortly after the deal was announced, it was speculated that Norris had pushed himself into the region of the money that is being earned by likes of F1 superstars Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

However, Norris has insisted that it is not the case.

“I mean, I feel I should earn as much as them, but it [his new contract] is certainly not close to the figures that I’ve been seeing online, sadly!” Norris said, as quoted by The Telegraph.

“Of course, it is a bit more [than the last deal], as it is with any job when you extend.

“But it’s certainly not close to the level of Lewis or Max. Which, in a way, it shouldn’t be because I’ve not achieved as much as what they’ve achieved in their careers.”

Having established themselves as two of F1's most successful drivers, it is no surprise that Verstappen and Hamilton are the two highest earners on the grid, who are estimated to be earning in the region of $60-70 million per year.

Norris has set his sights on reaching such figures, believing that in his current form, he can beat them head-to-head.

“But in another way, I believe it should be, because I believe I can fight against them whenever I need to, and I can do a better job whenever I need to. So yeah, I guess I have two opinions on it,” he said.

“I’m working on it. I don’t know when my next extension or renewal will be, but hopefully I can try and match [them] one day.

“But no, I dream of seeing those figures that I’ve seen online.”

title: Liam Lawson handed 'mentally tougher' verdict after Red Bull axe
excerpt:
Former Haas F1 team principal Guenther Steiner believes Liam Lawson is “mentally tougher” as a result of his demotion from Red Bull last year.

Lawson lasted just two rounds at the Milton Keynes-based squad last year as he struggled for form alongside Max Verstappen.

However, he got a second chance last time out at the Dutch Grand Prix as he was called up to replace an injured Isack Hadjar.

The New Zealander impressed as he lapped close to Verstappen before ending the race in seventh place, adding more points to his tally.

Steiner detailed the performance showcased how much more confidence he now possesses compared to 18 months ago.

“Last year's car was difficult to drive for anybody,” Steiner told the Red Flags podcast.

“I would also say Liam was not given enough time, as well. He has another year under his belt.

“What he went through there made him tougher mentally, because that's not easy to [endure].

“And now he goes in a Red Bull and has got quite a good level of confidence.”

One major difference at Red Bull this year is the absence of Helmut Marko, who was often very strict when it came to driver line-ups.

Steiner believes Marko's exit at the end of 2025 has put less pressure on Lawson's shoulders.

“He doesn't need to look over his shoulder all the time because one guy is not there anymore as well, which always was asking immediately if somebody wasn't bringing the performance,” he said.

“It was just also yet more experience, a different car. I think they are a little bit easier to drive than the cars from last year, the ground effect cars.

“Mentally, he was like 'I cannot lose here. I do the best with what I can. I don't focus on Max. I do my thing and try to do the best'.

“A lot of little things coming together, and all of a sudden it worked.”

title: Red Bull announce signing of senior Aston Martin figure to replace Gianpiero Lambiase
excerpt:
Red Bull has announced the signing of Tom McCullough from Aston Martin as its future head of racing.

He will join the Milton Keynes-based team in early 2027, after serving a period of gardenning leave from the Aston Martin group, and be the de facto replacement for the outgoing Gianpiero Lambiase, who will leave the team next year.

McCullough, who has enjoyed spells with Reynard Engineering, Williams, and Sauber, joined Aston Martin when it was Force India in 2014, originally as chief race engineer, before climbing to performance director in January 2018.

However, in January 2025, he was re-assigned from the F1 team after poor performances across the second-half of 2023 and through 2024, across to the performance directorship of Aston Martin Performance Technologies.

He was announced as leaving the Aston Martin group entirely in August 2026, and has now joined Red Bull in the newly-created role of 'head of racing.'

"We're delighted to welcome Tom to the team at the beginning of 2027, and look forward to the wealth of experience and expertise he will bring to the role," read a short Red Bull statement.

His signing is the second big-name Red Bull has lured from another team, after the capture of Gwen Lagrue from Mercedes as young driver advisor.

McCullough's signing comes as the team prepares for life after Lambiase, with the head of race engineering, and Max Verstappen's engineer, agreeing to join McLaren, with this expected to be from the 2028 season.

Other senior figures, such as chief designer Craig Skinner have also left, with a reshuffle seeing Ben Waterhouse becoming chief performance and design engineer, with Andrea Landi joining from Racing Bulls as head of performance.

title: Car flip and F1's closest ever finish: Five dramatic moments from the Italian GP
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix takes place this weekend, and it has served up its fair share of dramatic moments throughout its history.

Monza has a unique ability to deliver chaos, heartbreak and euphoria in equal measure. Few circuits on the calendar can match the sheer emotional range of the Italian Grand Prix, a race that has, time and again, produced moments that define entire eras of the sport.

As Ferrari's Charles Leclerc put it ahead of the 2025 edition of the race: "Monza is Monza, and I'll never stop trying. Winning on this track, in front of our tifosi, is so special that I can only have one goal this weekend."

But that emotional pull extends well beyond the Scuderia.

Here are five moments that encapsulate why the Italian Grand Prix remains one of the most dramatic fixtures on the F1 calendar.

The closest finish in F1 history, 1971

Before chicanes were installed to tame Monza's fearsome speeds, the old circuit was a slipstreaming playground.

The 1971 Italian Grand Prix remains the ultimate example. Peter Gethin, who started 11th, fought his way through a pack of cars that swapped positions relentlessly across 55 laps, with around 25 lead changes involving eight different drivers.

On the final lap, Gethin over-revved his BRM V12 engine out of Parabolica and edged ahead to beat Ronnie Peterson by just 0.01 seconds.

The top five were separated by a mere 0.61 seconds. It was Gethin's only F1 victory, and it remains the closest finish the sport has ever seen.

Senna's backmarker heartbreak denies McLaren a perfect season, 1988

McLaren had won every single race of the 1988 season heading into Monza, and Ayrton Senna looked set to continue that dominance and complete an unprecedented clean sweep.

With just two laps remaining, Senna led comfortably when he moved to lap Jean-Louis Schlesser's Williams at the Rettifilo chicane. Schlesser, substituting for the unwell Nigel Mansell, cut back unexpectedly and made contact with the McLaren's right rear, breaking its suspension and beaching Senna on a kerb.

Gerhard Berger and Michele Alboreto swept through in their Ferraris to complete a stunning 1-2, less than a month after Enzo Ferrari's death on 14 August.

McLaren finished the season with 15 wins from 16 races, an all-time record for dominance, but Monza ensured that a perfect, 16-from-16 season would remain forever out of reach.

Fittipaldi's last-lap backflip stuns Monza, 1993

The 1993 Italian Grand Prix produced one of the most astonishing moments ever witnessed at a finish line.

Running in eighth place on the final lap, Christian Fittipaldi attempted to overtake his own Minardi teammate Pierluigi Martini for seventh position down the main straight at close to 300 km/h.

As he pulled alongside, his left-front wheel clipped Martini's right-rear, and the impact acted as a ramp, launching Fittipaldi's car into the air and sending it through a full backward somersault.

The Minardi landed back on all four wheels, still pointing in the right direction, and skidded across the finish line. Fittipaldi was classified eighth. Neither driver was injured, and the moment remains one of the most spectacular in the sport's history.

Hamilton's pit lane blunder gifts Gasly a fairy tale, 2020

Lewis Hamilton was cruising to a comfortable victory at the 2020 Italian Grand Prix when Kevin Magnussen's retirement brought out the Safety Car.

Race control closed the pit lane, but Hamilton pitted regardless, the result of a communication breakdown with his Mercedes team. The resulting 10-second stop-and-go penalty dropped him to last.

A red flag for Charles Leclerc's heavy crash at Parabolica further reshuffled the order, and when the dust settled, Pierre Gasly found himself leading for AlphaTauri.

He held off Carlos Sainz by just 0.415 seconds to take a remarkable maiden victory, the team's first win since Sebastian Vettel triumphed at the same circuit in 2008.

Verstappen lands on Hamilton, 2021

The 2021 championship battle between Max Verstappen and Hamilton reached boiling point at Monza. After slow pit stops dropped both into each other's path, they arrived side by side at the Turn 1-2 chicane on lap 26.

Verstappen, attempting to pass around the outside, was squeezed towards the inside kerb at Turn 2, where his Red Bull struck the notorious sausage kerb and was launched into the air, landing directly on top of Hamilton's Mercedes.

The halo device was widely credited with preventing serious injury. Both retired on the spot, and stewards later judged Verstappen predominantly at fault, handing him a three-place grid penalty for the following race.

Daniel Ricciardo, meanwhile, led Lando Norris home for a McLaren 1-2, their first victory since 2012.

title: Honda outline Italian GP priority ahead of 'realistic' test
excerpt:
Honda has outlined its primary focus for the Italian Grand Prix this weekend as it gets its upgraded power unit back on track at Monza.

The Japanese manufacturer finally unveiled its new engine last time out at Zandvoort as it continues to make progress following its difficult start to the new season.

Its upgraded power unit came shortly after Aston Martin introduced a substantially modified package of its own.

Having lifted itself off the bottom of the standings, Aston Martin-Honda is seeking to get involved in regular contention for the point-scoring results.

However, with Monza being heavily reliant on strong straight-line speed, Honda insisted it must be “realistic” about the weekend ahead.

“Monza is a unique circuit with one of the highest full-throttle ratios on the 2026 calendar, with its long straights and only 11 corners,” said Honda's chief F1 engineer Shintaro Orihara.

“At this track, how you distribute the limited energy across these sections becomes crucial, and this is especially amplified in qualifying.

“The lap times at Monza are highly sensitive to power. With the introduction of our spec 2 engine in Zandvoort, we have made a step forward in terms of performance, but we need to be realistic about the upcoming weekend as we know that we are still behind our competitors in terms of overall power.”

Aston Martin managed to get itself into the points last time out in the Netherlands, with Fernando Alonso crossing the line in ninth place.

However, Honda has suggested it will not be focusing primarily on the results at Monza as it looks to improve the drivability of its engine.

“Our key focus at the Italian Grand Prix is to improve driveability,” Orihara said.

“Since the Dutch Grand Prix, we have been working a lot on the dyno at HRC Sakura to improve this and, specifically, to achieve stable and consistent combustion control.

“At Monza, we will be confirming the effect of that work and carrying out further tuning, which will give us more competitiveness in the coming races.”

title: Colton Herta handed latest F1 opportunity by Cadillac
excerpt:
Colton Herta will take part in the opening practice session this weekend at Monza for Cadillac, the team has confirmed.

Herta joined the American squad as a test and development driver for the 2026 campaign, which came with the guarantee of several FP1 outings.

Having stepped into the cockpit already in Barcelona and Hungary, Herta will have his third outing of the year this weekend at the Italian Grand Prix.

The 26-year-old will take over driving duties from Sergio Perez before the latter returns to the seat for FP2.

“This is an excellent opportunity to experience different aspects of the MAC-26,” Herta said.

“Having driven on the high-downforce tracks in Barcelona and Budapest, the challenge will be very different in Monza.

“With the car set up for low drag, it will move around more, placing a greater emphasis on accuracy at the braking points and on threading the eye of a needle across the curbs in the chicanes.

“I’m really excited to be able to contribute to the race weekend and to the team’s further development at one of the most iconic circuits in motorsport.”

Herta is vying for a full-time seat with Cadillac in 2027, and his F1 outing will coincide with his F2 programme that continues this weekend at Monza.

title: McLaren confirm return of eye-catching F1 upgrade at Italian GP
excerpt:
McLaren has confirmed it will race its rotating 'Macarena' rear wing at the Italian Grand Prix, giving the concept its first competitive outing on the MCL40.

The team calls its version the H-Wing, a nod to the 'H' in Etihad Airways branding on the rear wing.

The team has detailed it mirrors the logic behind McLaren's 2010 F-duct name, which came from the Vodafone 'F' placed near the MP4-25's air inlet.

The concept first ran in practice at the Hungarian Grand Prix, when reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli evaluated it on Oscar Piastri's car in FP1.

That test focused on controlled aero runs and braking checks before the wing was removed ahead of qualifying. Andrea Stella described it as a "positive sign-off" and said McLaren was preparing to introduce it at future events.

It has now been confirmed it will be in use at Monza this weekend as McLaren continues to its momentum, having won two races on the bounce.

The Macarena wing was first spotted at pre-season testing by Ferrari and has since been adopted by Red Bull - albeit the design has been sidelined following a series of high-speed spins for Max Verstappen.

“This weekend, we have brought what we believe is needed to be competitive, including a new low-drag rear wing specification, including the first use of our H-Wing, alongside some small aerodynamic and low-drag options that we will evaluate before deciding the final specification for Qualifying,” technical director Neil Houdley said.

“Overall, we know there is still more performance to unlock from the MCL40, both through maximising the package we already have and through further upgrades planned for the races ahead.”
